extracted.intended_audience: Tuskegee graduates, Negro educators, and community leaders in the rural South (early 20th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for Tuskegee graduates and Negro teachers on how to educate and uplift rural Black communities—what work to do, the aims of education, measures of institutional and individual success, and warnings about pitfalls. Emphasis is on practical, applied industrial/agricultural education and community leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending education to the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: One of two distinct problems facing the Tuskegee graduate: the problem of extending education to the masses of our people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates should go into rural sections to teach and persuade communities to value schooling; institutions and graduates must work to lengthen school terms, keep children in school, and arouse interest in education through committees and direct community engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting people to actual conditions for racial harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: One of two distinct problems facing the Tuskegee graduate: the problem of so adjusting the people to their actual conditions that the two races will be able to live and work together in harmony and helpfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work includes teaching practical skills, promoting frugality and thrift, encouraging land ownership and self-reliance so communities can better coexist and participate in regional economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the beauty and dignity of all labor; emphasize agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim of the institution: to teach the beauty and dignity of all labor and inculcate a love for the soil and for agricultural life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many students come from farming sections, put stress upon agriculture and show that country life offers superior opportunities; education should dignify manual and agricultural labor rather than aiming solely to remove people from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train leaders imbued with sacrifice and service
rubrics_metrics.description: Train leaders for the masses of our people; need young men and women imbued with the spirit of sacrifice and service who will teach how to live economically, pay debts, buy land, and build better homes and schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates should be prepared morally and practically to lead rural improvement efforts and to model upright life; leadership measured by tangible community uplift (schools, homes, churches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Train high-class domestic servants and practical vocational roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of institutional aims: to train a high class of domestic servants as well as practical workers (teachers, farmers, mechanics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is ample material for vocational training; success judged by graduates' competence and reputation in practical occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional worth judged by service to practical daily needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth of an institution is not determined by acquisition of houses and land, nor by the bare statement of its aims, but by its actual power to serve the practical, daily needs of the community in which it exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure institutional success by concrete community outcomes (extended school terms, land ownership increases, improved houses and churches, cordial race relations), not merely by property or proclamations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible outcomes as metrics of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of success: graduates doing creditable work as teachers, farmers, mechanics, and domestic workers; more than fifty percent bought homes; students prompted communities to lengthen terms and build better structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graduate follow-up (occupation, home ownership), community adoption of educational improvements, and local economic improvements as indicators of institutional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community improvement via organized incentives (Black Belt Improvement Society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an organized society with graded membership and prizes to stimulate property ownership, better farming, gardens, better houses, and land purchases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership degrees tied to ownership (chickens/pigs → cow → acre → house → increasing acreage) and annual fairs/prizes create social incentives; committees (education, labor, farming, good government, business, good roads) carry out targeted improvement work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must manifest itself in practical daily life
rubrics_metrics.description: Any education which did not manifest itself in the practical daily life of the people was not worthy of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should be directly applicable—students must be able to use learning on the farm, in trade, or in home and community life. The principal idea (Booker Washington's) is timely: education to dignify and make attractive country life and fit people for useful citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaken aims of education (not to merely free from manual labor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the view that education's end is to free one from manual labor or to fit people only for teacher, preacher, or politician; such a conception was a mistake in the Black-Belt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize broad practical education that strengthens rural life and citizenship rather than encouraging unnecessary urban migration or narrow professional hopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardships and offences produce strength and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardships, trials, persecution, and offences are primary necessities that produce patience, self-reliance, self-sacrifice and virtues making for true manhood and womanhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret historical suffering as having produced institutions (churches, schools, businesses) and virtues; use this as moral scaffolding for community uplift and perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of loyalty and civic contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of the Negro's regard for the nation: loyalty in war (willingness to fight and die), participation in Liberty Loan, Red Cross, War Savings Stamp drives, and industrial/civil contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loyalty is expressed through military service, buying bonds, supporting relief efforts, and avoiding strikes during national emergency; such actions are cited to claim equal share in democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postwar demands for equal civil and legal rights
rubrics_metrics.description: List of concrete questions/claims expected after the war: share in democracy; end lynchings; fair trials with juries including Negroes; end taxation without representation; equal education funding; fair employment; access to lodging when travelling; courteous treatment by transport staff; voting rights for those meeting qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standards by which the Negro community will judge whether the nation practices democracy for all; they are demands for equal protection and opportunity across legal, educational, and civic spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go to the masses (prioritize work among the rural poor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduates are warned not to remain ‘on the mountain’ (in admired elevated positions) but must go down among the masses where the harvest is great and laborers few—the work of the world must be done at the foot of the mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspiring leaders should choose service in rural districts and settlement work over seeking prestige; the locus of service is where needs are greatest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society should be built on merit and character, not display
rubrics_metrics.description: Negro society is often built upon display and shadow rather than merit and substance; the aim should be to base society on character and real achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders and teachers should foster confidence, sound moral character, and purposeful economic behavior rather than ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear purpose and persistent resolve
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men and women need purpose—being more interested in making a dollar than in spending one—and the spirit of perseverance (illustrated by Grant's unceasing command 'On to Richmond').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an unwavering purpose and resolve in the face of hardships; sustained, focused effort yields victory and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must be applied, assimilated, and embodied
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, in order to be real, must be applied; it must be digested and assimilated and become part of your flesh and blood so you are transformed and then go out and live it among the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely theoretical learning; require practice, habits, and moral internalization so teachings produce observable behavioral change in graduates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher preparation for child and institutional problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must be prepared to deal with problems of the child (backward children, abnormal children, the blind, the deaf, incorrigibles, the feeble minded) and must be qualified for elementary, secondary, and collegiate grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional preparation should include methods for special needs, grade-specific pedagogy, and contextual strategies to make school fit the student's social and economic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic security necessary for effective teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: No teacher can do his best so long as there is doubt and uncertainty about his daily bread; the Negro teacher's burden is two-fold because he must also worry about bread-and-butter concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure stable compensation and living conditions for teachers to enable full professional commitment and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative: build schools and persuade communities
rubrics_metrics.description: A rural teacher must not find ways prepared for him; he must make a way, build school-houses, persuade and organize the people to extend terms and support education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers are expected to be community organizers—raising funds, mobilizing interest, constructing facilities, and persuading families to send children to school.
